summary: Hebrew has one present tense, and it works differently from Greek, German or Russian: the verb does not change for the person (I / you / he) but for **gender and number** — four forms. אָכַל “to eat”: אוֹכֵל for a man or a masculine subject, אוֹכֶלֶת for a woman, אוֹכְלִים for men or a mixed group, אוֹכְלוֹת for women only. The person is shown only by the subject, so the pronoun is never left out: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל, אַתָּה אוֹכֵל and הוּא אוֹכֵל share one form. The present is historically a participle (בֵּינוֹנִי, “the middle form”), which is why it inflects like an adjective. One form covers “I eat” and “I am eating” — there is no progressive and no helper verb “do”. The vowels depend on the verb’s pattern (binyan, see roots and patterns): paʿal אוֹכֵל, שׁוֹתֶה; piʿel מְבַשֵּׁל. After רוֹצֶה “want” or אוֹהֵב “like”, a second verb is an infinitive with לְ־: אֲנִי רוֹצֶה לֶאֱכֹל, הִיא אוֹהֶבֶת לְבַשֵּׁל. The past and the future do have person endings; they come after the foundations (C01, C02).

blocks.title: Gender and number, not person
blocks.text: The present form tells you whether the subject is masculine or feminine, one or more — never whether it is “I”, “you” or “he”. That is why the pronoun (or a noun) must always be there: אֲנִי שׁוֹתֶה, אַתָּה שׁוֹתֶה, הוּא שׁוֹתֶה.

blocks.title: Who is “I”?
blocks.text: A woman says אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת, אֲנִי רוֹצָה; a man אֲנִי אוֹכֵל, אֲנִי רוֹצֶה. Speaking to a woman: אַתְּ שׁוֹתָה. A group with even one man takes the masculine plural: הֵם אוֹכְלִים.

blocks.title: One form, two meanings — and no “do”
blocks.text: הִיא שׁוֹתָה קָפֶה is “she drinks coffee” and “she is drinking coffee”. A question is the same sentence with a question mark: אַתָּה שׁוֹתֶה קָפֶה? “Do you drink coffee?”

items: Masculine or feminine? One or more?
blocks.caption: Building a present-tense sentence

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Who is speaking, and to whom (man or woman)?
One person or more? Is there a man in the group?
Is there a second verb after רוֹצֶה / אוֹהֵב? → the infinitive.

askYourself: Who does it? → put the pronoun or the noun first; in the present the pronoun is never left out.
Is the subject masculine or feminine? (For אֲנִי and אַתָּה / אַתְּ it depends on who speaks and to whom.)
One or more? A mixed group → masculine plural (-ִים).
Which pattern? A root ending in ה → -ֶה / -ָה (שׁוֹתֶה, שׁוֹתָה); piʿel → מְ־ in front (מְבַשֵּׁל); otherwise like אוֹכֵל.
Is there a second verb after רוֹצֶה / אוֹהֵב? → the infinitive with לְ־: לֶאֱכֹל, לִשְׁתּוֹת, לְבַשֵּׁל.
Is it a question? → the same form, no “do”: אַתָּה אוֹכֵל?
steps: Find the subject’s gender and number.
Put the object after the verb (with אֶת when it is definite).

traps: *אֲנִי אוֹכֵל said by a woman — she says אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת.
*הִיא שׁוֹתֶלֶת — when the root ends in ה the feminine ends in -ָה: שׁוֹתָה, רוֹצָה, קוֹנָה.
*אוֹכֵל לֶחֶם for “I eat bread” — in the present the pronoun is required: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל לֶחֶם.
A group of women with one man is masculine: הֵם אוֹכְלִים, אֲנַחְנוּ שׁוֹתִים.
רוֹצָה “she wants” ≠ רָצְתָה “she wanted”; קוֹנָה “she buys” ≠ קָנְתָה “she bought”.
No progressive: “I am eating” is just אֲנִי אוֹכֵל — no form of הָיָה.
*רוֹצֶה אוֹכֵל — after רוֹצֶה the second verb is the infinitive: רוֹצֶה לֶאֱכֹל.

seeAlso.note: Arabic’s present (the imperfect) marks the person with prefixes and also gender and number — يَأْكُلُ, تَأْكُلُ, آكُلُ …; the Hebrew present has no person at all, only four gender-number forms.
German conjugates by person and number (ich esse, du isst, er isst …) and never by gender — the reverse of the Hebrew present.
Chinese verbs never change: 我吃, 她吃, 他们吃 — time and aspect come from other words.
